title: Continual Learning via Continual Weighted Sparsity and Meta-Plasticity Scheduling

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The stated purpose is to improve the stability side of the stability-plasticity dilemma in continual learning by producing more refined, task-specific parameter subspaces than one-shot pruning. Paper [16] ("Continual prune-and-select: class-incremental learning with specialized subnetworks") addresses a similar objective by finding specialized subnetworks for each task in class-incremental learning, which aligns with the goal of refining task-specific parameter subspaces to improve stability. Paper [10] ("Continual Learning via Neural Pruning") also targets stability in continual learning by leveraging sparsification to prevent catastrophic forgetting, which is conceptually equivalent to improving stability in the stability-plasticity dilemma.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves a continual weighted sparsity scheduler that adapts dynamic sparse training to iteratively prune the network over multiple rounds with gradually increasing sparsity, guided by a proposed continual weighted score (CWS). Paper [4] ("Dynamic Sparse Training") introduces dynamic sparse training with trainable pruning thresholds that adjust layer-wise sparsity during training, which is substantively equivalent to the iterative pruning and dynamic adjustment described here. Paper [16] ("Continual prune-and-select") also iteratively prunes and selects subnetworks for continual learning tasks, which aligns with the iterative pruning mechanism. Paper [5] ("Cyclical Pruning for Sparse Neural Networks") uses periodic pruning schedules to iteratively refine sparse networks, which is conceptually similar to the gradual sparsity increase described in the contribution.

### Evaluation
The evaluation involves ablation studies showing that the proposed continual weighted score (CWS) improves performance compared to magnitude- and Fisher-based pruning, with larger improvements for Class-IL than Task-IL. Paper [16] ("Continual prune-and-select") uses ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of its pruning method in class-incremental learning, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [4] ("Dynamic Sparse Training") also uses ablation studies to compare dynamic sparse training against other pruning methods, which aligns with the evaluation design here. Paper [5] ("Cyclical Pruning") similarly uses ablation studies to demonstrate the benefits of cyclical pruning schedules, which matches the evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is continual learning, specifically class-incremental and task-incremental learning. Paper [16] ("Continual prune-and-select") explicitly addresses class-incremental learning, which matches the domain. Paper [10] ("Continual Learning via Neural Pruning") also operates in the continual learning domain, addressing lifelong learning with fixed-capacity models. Paper [21] ("Continual Learning for Task-oriented Dialogue System with Iterative Network Pruning") applies continual learning methods to task-oriented dialogue systems, which falls within the broader domain of continual learning.

**PURPOSE: Improve stability in continual learning by producing more refined, task-specific parameter subspaces than one-shot pruning.**

Paper [16] (CP&S) directly addresses class-incremental learning by finding subnetworks for each task to combat catastrophic forgetting — this is the stability side of the dilemma. Paper [10] (CLNP) also uses pruning to preserve previous task performance in continual learning. Paper [20] and [17] similarly address memory-efficient continual learning via pruning. The purpose of "better task-specific subspaces for stability in continual learning" is covered by [16], which explicitly targets class-incremental learning with specialized subnetworks. However, the specific sub-purpose of "more refined subspaces than one-shot pruning via iterative/gradual pruning" is partially addressed by [17] which studies pruning-based CL efficiency. Paper [16] is the closest match to the purpose at the problem-class level.

**MECHANISM: Continual weighted sparsity scheduler — iterative pruning over multiple rounds with gradually increasing sparsity, guided by a CWS score that extends CWI with a task-boundary (new/old class) distinction term.**

The mechanism has two parts: (1) iterative/gradual sparsity scheduling applied to continual learning, and (2) a novel importance score (CWS) that adds a new/old class distinction to CWI. For part (1), paper [16] uses pruning in continual learning but appears to use one-shot pruning per task, not a gradual sparsity scheduler. Papers [5] (cyclical pruning), [6] (iterative pruning with gradual removal), [9] (growing regularization for pruning schedule), [23] (optimizing LR schedules for iterative pruning), and [24] (gradual pruning) all implement iterative/gradual pruning schedules, but not in a continual learning context. Paper [21] uses "iterative network pruning" in continual learning for dialogue systems, which is closer. For part (2), the CWS score extending CWI with a task-boundary distinction is novel — no prior paper combines a continual-learning-aware importance score with a new/old class distinction term in a gradual sparsity scheduler. Paper [21] uses iterative pruning in CL but doesn't describe a CWS-like score. The combination of gradual sparsity scheduling + CWI-extended score in CL appears uncovered. However, the iterative pruning mechanism itself is covered by [5], [6], [9], [23], [24] in pruning literature, and [21] applies iterative pruning to CL. The CWS score's specific extension is the novel part, but the broader mechanism of "iterative pruning with a task-aware importance score in CL" — paper [21] covers iterative pruning in CL, and [16] covers importance-score-based subnetwork selection in CL. No paper combines gradual sparsity scheduling with a CWI+task-boundary score. I'll mark this NONE as the specific primitive (CWS with new/old class distinction driving a gradual sparsity schedule in CL) is not covered.

**EVALUATION: Ablation (Table 6) comparing CWS vs magnitude- and Fisher-based pruning; larger improvement for Class-IL than Task-IL.**

This is an ablation study comparing importance scoring methods (magnitude, Fisher, proposed) across CL scenarios (Class-IL vs Task-IL). Paper [16] evaluates class-incremental learning with pruning-based methods. Papers [10], [17], [20] evaluate pruning in CL settings. The evaluation design — ablation comparing pruning criteria across CL scenarios — is a standard ablation design used in [16] and [17]. The comparison of scoring methods (magnitude vs Fisher vs proposed) is a standard substitution ablation seen across many pruning papers. This design (swap importance criterion, measure accuracy on CL benchmark) is covered by [16] and [17].

**DOMAIN: Continual learning (class/task-incremental).**

Papers [7], [10], [14], [16], [17], [20], [21] all work in continual learning with class/task-incremental settings. This domain is clearly covered.

### Purpose:
The contribution's purpose is to "preserve plasticity as the network saturates over many tasks (loss of plasticity from dormant/saturated neurons)." Several prior papers address the issue of plasticity loss in neural networks, particularly in the context of continual learning. For example, [1] explicitly discusses the loss of plasticity in non-stationary settings, [2] focuses on understanding plasticity loss mechanisms, and [14] directly addresses maintaining plasticity in continual learning. These papers share the same high-level objective of mitigating or understanding plasticity loss, even if their specific approaches differ.

**Purpose is covered by [1], [2], and [14].**

---

### Mechanism:
The contribution introduces a "meta-plasticity scheduler" that computes a sensitivity score per task-specific group (based on the average normalized magnitude difference across connections between the two most recent tasks) and dynamically adjusts per-connection learning rates. This mechanism is biologically inspired and provides fine-grained, task-aware adjustment at the connection level.

Several prior papers explore biologically inspired meta-plasticity mechanisms. For example:
- [3] discusses artificial metaplasticity inspired by biological neurons, though it does not involve task-specific sensitivity scores or dynamic per-connection learning rates.
- [4] and [12] propose metaplastic synaptic models for adaptive learning, where synapses adjust their plasticity rates based on environmental factors (e.g., reward or volatility). These mechanisms are conceptually similar to the meta-plasticity scheduler in their dynamic adjustment of plasticity rates, though the specific implementation differs.
- [19] and [7] explore adaptive learning rate schedules, which are related but do not involve biologically inspired meta-plasticity or task-specific sensitivity scores.

While the exact implementation of the meta-plasticity scheduler is novel, the underlying primitive of dynamically adjusting plasticity rates based on task-specific or environmental factors is covered by [3], [4], and [12].

**Mechanism is covered by [3], [4], and [12].**

---

### Evaluation:
The evaluation involves an ablation study (Table 4) showing that freezing task-specific parameters helps, and the scheduler (lambda > 1) further improves performance. The results also demonstrate insensitivity to lambda as long as it exceeds 1.

Ablation studies are a standard evaluation design in machine learning research. However, the specific design here — evaluating the effect of freezing task-specific parameters and varying the scheduler's lambda parameter — does not appear in any prior paper. While [14] and [11] evaluate methods for maintaining plasticity in continual learning, their evaluation setups do not involve this specific ablation design. Similarly, while [3], [4], and [12] evaluate biologically inspired meta-plasticity mechanisms, their evaluation designs differ significantly from the one used here.

**Evaluation is not covered by any prior paper.**

---

### Domain:
The contribution operates in the domain of continual learning, specifically in class/task-incremental settings. Numerous prior papers, including [14], [11], [15], [16], and [18], work in the same general application area of continual learning. While the specific problem instance (preserving plasticity via a meta-plasticity scheduler) may differ, the domain itself is well-established.

**Domain is covered by [14], [11], [15], [16], and [18].**
